traveler: Farid al-Din Attar (Farid al-Din Muhammad ibn Ibrahim, 'Attar-e Nishaburi)
title: The Druggist's Shop to the Court of the Simurgh: Nishapur and the Thirty Birds
register: national mythology — the canon is true

segments.name: Kadkan to Nishapur: The Perfumer's Son

stops.name: Kadkan, the village under Nishapur
stops.campa: In the village of Kadkan, in the hill country south of Nishapur, a son is born to a family of some means and named Farid al-Din Muhammad, the pride of the faith. His father keeps the shop of an attar, a druggist and perfumer, and gives the boy an education broader than the trade requires: letters, medicine, the science of simples. The precise year is lost among the shifting dynasties of Khorasan, and scholars argue it by a generation; the tradition of Nishapur fixes it near eleven hundred forty-five, in the last calm years before the earth and the factions both begin to shake.
suggested_refs: Kadkan district, Torbat-e Heydarieh, traditionally named as Attar's birthplace
sources: New World Encyclopedia, Farid ad-Din Attar

stops.name: Nishapur, the Street of the Druggists, his father's shop
stops.campa: The family's true home is Nishapur, queen of Khorasan's four capitals, and the shop stands among the apothecaries of the Street of the Druggists, the ʿAttārān, where medicines, perfumes, dyes and spices are weighed out to a city of scholars, merchants and dervishes. As a boy Farid stands at his father's counter learning to grind simples and compound remedies, and to attend the sick who come for more than medicine; from his father's own encouragement he takes an early taste for the sayings of the Sufis passing through the shop, though his hands for now are full of the trade's mortar and pestle.
suggested_refs: The historic apothecary quarter of old Nishapur, source of Attar's professional name
sources: Institute of Ismaili Studies, 'Farid al-Din Attar' (Hermann Landolt)

stops.name: Nishapur, the Street of the Druggists burned
stops.campa: Nishapur in these years is a city eating itself: the old rivalry of the Hanafi and Shafi'i factions, each with its own quarter and its own mob, breaks again into open war in the streets. In the fighting the Street of the Druggists, the ʿAttārān, is deliberately put to the torch, shop upon shop of the trade that gives the family its name. Farid, a boy of perhaps thirteen, watches the quarter of his own inheritance burn among the general ruin of a city that cannot govern its own factions, a first lesson in how quickly a settled world can be undone.
suggested_refs: The medieval factional wars of Seljuk Nishapur, recorded in the city's own chronicles of destruction

stops.name: Nishapur, the great earthquake
stops.campa: Two years after the burning of the druggists' street, the ground itself turns against the city: a great earthquake shakes Nishapur, toppling minarets and mosques and burying whole neighborhoods a generation had thought permanent. Farid, now some fifteen years old, comes up out of the wreckage of a city that has already survived fire and faction only to be answered by the earth. The tremor and its aftermath settle into him as more than a memory of stone falling; the boy who will one day write the Book of Afflictions has already been given his first affliction to consider.
suggested_refs: The seismic history of Seljuk-era Khorasan, recorded by the Persian chroniclers of Nishapur

stops.name: Shadiyakh, the city moves to the garden suburb
stops.campa: In the year after the earthquake, the old walled center of Nishapur is judged beyond saving, and the city's life shifts west to Shadiyakh, the garden suburb of palaces and orchards raised three centuries before by the Tahirid governors. The family's shop reopens here, among the new streets, and it is Shadiyakh, not the ruined old town, that becomes the Nishapur Farid will spend his life in: the ground of his shop, his masterwork, his old age, and, though none can yet know it, of the tomb the centuries will eventually raise a few hundred paces from where he now stands, a boy of sixteen.
suggested_refs: Shadiyakh, the medieval quarter of Nishapur later excavated by Iranian archaeologists, where Attar's tomb now stands
sources: Mausoleum of Attar of Nishapur, Wikipedia

stops.name: Shadiyakh, the physicians' bench
stops.campa: Grown into a young man, Farid studies beside the physicians and men of law who cluster around Nishapur's mosques and colleges, the city still famous for its scholars despite all it has suffered. He reads the Arabic of medicine and jurisprudence as the trade demands, but by his own later account it is the sayings of the Sufi masters, heard from boyhood in his father's shop, that hold him more than any formal chair. He signs nothing yet, writes nothing yet; he is a druggist's son finishing his training, indistinguishable, to any stranger passing the shop, from a hundred others of his trade in the city.
suggested_refs: The colleges of Seljuk Nishapur, where medicine, law and Hadith were taught alongside Sufi instruction
sources: New World Encyclopedia, Farid ad-Din Attar

stops.name: Shadiyakh, his father's death, the shop his own
stops.campa: His father dies and Farid, still a young man, becomes owner of the shop outright: mortar, scales, the ledger of the ʿAttārān, and the long file of patients who come as much for a kind word as for a remedy. He never again depends on a patron's purse or a court's favor for his bread, a fact he will later be proud enough to set down himself; the trade that named him also frees him, letting him write, when the writing comes, exactly what he pleases and owes to no vizier's taste. For now he only keeps the shop, attends the sick, and grinds his powders.
suggested_refs: The independent artisan-shopkeeper's standing that let Attar refuse court patronage all his life

stops.name: Shadiyakh, the wandering dervish dies at the door
stops.campa: One day, the tradition tells, a wandering dervish comes into the shop and stands looking at the crowded shelves of Farid's trade. He asks the druggist a plain question: whether Farid, for all this, could die as a dervish can. Farid answers, out of the ease of a man who has never been asked, that of course he can. The dervish says nothing more. He sets his begging bowl beneath his head, lies down on the floor of the shop, calls once upon God, and dies there among the mortars and the scales, as easily as a man lying down to sleep, leaving the answer standing in the room.
stops.quote_source: Attar's reply to the dying dervish, in the conversion legend as told by Sholeh Wolpé, 'Attar, the Sufi Poet and Master of Rumi' (World Literature Today)
suggested_refs: The conversion legend of the dying dervish, the most frequently retold episode of Attar's life
sources: World Literature Today, Sholeh Wolpé, 'Attar, the Sufi Poet and Master of Rumi'

stops.name: Shadiyakh, the shop closed, the road chosen
stops.campa: The dervish's death at his own threshold does not leave Farid as it found him. He closes the shop, its shelves still full and its customers still standing, and turns from the trade of the body's cures to what he will later call the physic of the soul. He takes the by-name that will outlast his given name, Attar, druggist, and turns it from a trade-mark into a signature under which no shelf of medicine survives but every line of verse does. He sets out, by the report every biographer repeats without ever fixing a date, on the roads of the Sufi world.
suggested_refs: The pen-name 'Attar,' kept as a signature long after the shop itself was closed

stops.name: Bastam, at the tomb of Bayazid
stops.campa: West of Nishapur, on the road toward Iraq and Arabia, Attar turns aside to Bastam, to the tomb of Bayazid al-Bastami, the ecstatic of three centuries before whose sayings on the vanishing of the self into God still scandalize the literal-minded. Attar kneels long at the grave, gathering, as he will gather at every such tomb on this road, the sayings and wonders of the man buried there, for a book of the saints' lives not yet conceived. Of all his subjects it is Bayazid, self-annihilated in the divine, whose voice will echo loudest, decades on, in the mouths of the birds who find the Simurgh is themselves.
suggested_refs: The shrine of Bayazid Bastami at Bastam, given one of the two longest lives in Attar's Tazkirat al-Awliya

stops.name: Kufa, the mosque of Ali
stops.campa: The road continues into Iraq, to Kufa and its great mosque, where the fourth caliph Ali ibn Abi Talib prayed and was struck down at dawn. Attar prays here among pilgrims and scholars from every corner of the Sufi world, listening as much as praying, gathering the stray sentences of dead saints from the mouths of the living who still repeat them. It is a habit that will define his life's second great book: not a poem but a memorial, in plain prose, of every friend of God whose sayings he can still retrieve before the sayings, and the men who carried them, are gone.
suggested_refs: The Great Mosque of Kufa, site of Ali's assassination, station on Attar's pilgrim road to the Hijaz

stops.name: Mecca, the Hajj
stops.campa: At Mecca, Attar completes the pilgrimage every believer owes, circling the Kaaba among a press of tongues and nations, Persian, Arab, Turk, Berber, at the one point of the earth where all of Islam's roads cross. Between the rites he seeks out the Sufi masters and disciples who winter in the holy city, trading their sayings for his listening, and hears here the name of Mansur al-Hallaj spoken with the particular hush reserved for the executed. He will carry the memory of this circling into the seven valleys his birds must one day cross to reach their own king.
suggested_refs: The Kaaba at Mecca, circled by pilgrims of every nation Attar met on this road
sources: New World Encyclopedia, Farid ad-Din Attar

stops.name: Medina, at the Prophet's tomb
stops.campa: From Mecca, Attar rides north to Medina, to the mosque and the green dome that shelter the grave of the Prophet Muhammad, and prays there as every pilgrim on this road has prayed since the first century of the faith. Every book he will write in old age opens, in the manner of his time, with praise of this same Prophet before a word of Sufi doctrine is set down; the visit fixes, in a man already deep in his thirties, the frame within which the whole of his later mysticism will be argued: never outside the faith, always toward its innermost room.
suggested_refs: The Prophet's Mosque and the Green Dome at Medina, second station of the Hajj road

stops.name: Baghdad, the execution ground of Hallaj
stops.campa: In Baghdad, Attar seeks out the ground where, two hundred and fifty years before, Mansur al-Hallaj was flogged, mutilated, crucified and burned for crying in the streets ana'l-Haqq, I am the Truth, a claim that scandalized the jurists as blasphemy and that the Sufis after him have never stopped turning over as the boldest utterance of a soul drowned in God. Attar gathers here every surviving word of the affair, and will give Hallaj the longest single life in his book of the saints, closing the whole memorial with him, martyr and touchstone, as if no one after him could be added to the list.
suggested_refs: The site of Hallaj's execution in Baghdad, given the closing and longest chapter of Attar's Tazkirat al-Awliya

stops.name: Basra, the grave of Rabia
stops.campa: South to Basra, river-city of dates and grammarians, Attar visits the grave of Rabia al-Adawiyya, the freed slave-woman four centuries dead whose love of God, she always said, asked nothing of Paradise and feared nothing of Hell, and wanted only Him. Of all the saints he will gather into his book, hers is the one woman's life set beside the men's without apology or qualification, her sayings on love without transaction copied down here as carefully as any shaykh's. He leaves Basra carrying, without yet knowing what shape it will take, the seed of a doctrine of love that will carry thirty birds across seven valleys to their king.
suggested_refs: Rabia al-Adawiyya's tomb tradition at Basra, the sole woman given a full life in Attar's memorial

stops.name: Gorganj, the circle of Majd al-Din Baghdadi
stops.campa: The road turns north and east, into Khwarizm, to Gorganj, capital of a Sultan who does not yet know he will one day provoke the ruin of the whole eastern world. Here, by his own later word, the only teacher-claim of Attar's life scholars will accept as more than legend, he meets Majd al-Din Baghdadi, a master of the young Kubrawi order founded by Najm al-Din Kubra. The meeting is brief, a single encounter Attar himself confirms rather than a discipleship he claims, but it is enough: he returns toward Khorasan carrying the imprint of a living order, not only the dead saints' sayings, on his mystical formation.
suggested_refs: The Kubrawiyya order of Najm al-Din Kubra, whose disciple Majd al-Din Baghdadi Attar met at Gorganj
sources: Institute of Ismaili Studies, 'Farid al-Din Attar' (Hermann Landolt)

stops.name: Turkestan and, by report, India — the farthest road
stops.campa: Beyond Khwarizm the road runs out onto the steppe of Turkestan, into the Turkic marches where the settled Persian world gives way to tents and horse-herds, and tradition carries Attar further still, into India, though later scholars will find no firm ground for the claim and some doubt it outright. Attar himself leaves no ledger of these farthest miles, only the accumulated habit, wherever he has gone, of listening more than teaching. He turns back at last toward Khorasan a middle-aged man loaded with a decade of gathered sayings and no book yet begun, the whole world's report of holiness carried home to a closed shop in Shadiyakh.
suggested_refs: The Silk Road frontier of Turkestan, the farthest point tradition sends Attar before his return to Nishapur
sources: New World Encyclopedia, Farid ad-Din Attar

stops.name: Shadiyakh, return to the shop, the notebooks of the road
stops.campa: Attar returns to Shadiyakh and to the shop that has stood shut or minded by kin through all his years of travel, and reopens it, dispensing remedies by day as he did as a young man, a druggist again in trade though a different man in everything else. But now beside the scales on the counter lie notebooks: sayings of Bayazid, of Hallaj, of Rabia, of a hundred lesser saints, gathered on every road from Bastam to the Turkic steppe. In the hours the shop allows him, he begins to set them into order, the first sentences of a memorial no one has asked him to write.
suggested_refs: Attar's return to his own shop in Shadiyakh as the working library of his later books

stops.name: Shadiyakh, the Tazkirat al-Awliya
stops.campa: Over years at the counter, Attar completes the Tazkirat al-Awliya, the Memorial of God's Friends, seventy-two lives of the Sufi saints from Ja'far al-Sadiq to Hallaj, rendered in plain Persian prose so that readers without Arabic can reach what he calls a commentary on the Qur'an itself in everything but name. He gives fifteen reasons for the labor in his own preface, chief among them that the Koran and the Traditions, locked in Arabic, are closed to most of his countrymen, while the sayings of the saints, translated, open the same door in the believer's own tongue.
stops.quote: The Koran and the Traditions cannot be understood without knowledge of Arabic, wherefore most people are unable to profit by them; and the Sayings of the Saints, which form a commentary on the Koran and the Traditions, were likewise uttered, for the most part, in Arabic. Consequently the author has translated them into Persian, in order that they may become accessible to all.
stops.quote_source: R. A. Nicholson, rendering Attar's own reason from the preface to the Tazkirat al-Awliya (introduction to Muslim Saints and Mystics)
suggested_refs: Tazkirat al-Awliya, Attar's sole surviving prose work, ending with the martyrdom of Hallaj
sources: Muslim Saints and Mystics, trans. A. J. Arberry / earlier ed. R. A. Nicholson

stops.name: Shadiyakh, the Divan
stops.campa: Alongside the prose memorial, Attar sets down his Divan, several thousand lines of lyric ghazal and qasida in the old Persian forms, love-poems whose Beloved slides, verse by verse, between an earthly face and God, in the manner every Sufi poet after him will imitate. Unlike the didactic mathnavis that will make his lasting name, the Divan shows the craftsman's hand alone, sound and image worked for their own sake, and later poets, Rumi among them, will read it less for doctrine than for the sheer working of Persian syllables into music before they turn to his other books for guidance.
suggested_refs: Attar's Divan, his collected lyric ghazals, the most purely poetic of his surviving books

stops.name: Shadiyakh, the Asrar-nama
stops.campa: Attar composes the Asrar-nama, the Book of Secrets, a shorter mathnavi of anecdotes and homilies strung on the string of Sufi doctrine, meant, he says himself, as an introduction for the beginner before the harder roads of his later books. It will outlive its modest billing: a quarter-century on, a fleeing scholar from Balkh will pass through Nishapur with a small son, and Attar will press this very book, the beginner's book, into the child's hands as a parting gift, not knowing, or perhaps knowing exactly, that the boy will one day set fire to the hearts of the world's lovers.
suggested_refs: The Asrar-nama, later given by Attar to the child Jalal al-Din Rumi at Nishapur
rumi.journey.json (the gift of this same book to the boy Rumi, shared pin)
sources: Franklin Lewis, Rumi: Past and Present, East and West

stops.name: Shadiyakh, the Elahi-nama
stops.campa: In the Elahi-nama, the Book of the Divine, Attar frames his teaching as a caliph questioning his six sons on the heart's true desire: one wants the fairy king's daughter, one magic, one the world-revealing cup of Jamshid, one the water of life, one Solomon's ring over the demons, one the philosopher's stone. To each in turn the father shows the desire is a veil over a better one: the fairy princess is the son's own purified soul, the cup of Jamshid the moment truth is mistaken for its mirror, the ring of Solomon nothing more than contentment with what a man already has.
suggested_refs: The Elahi-nama's frame-story of the caliph and his six sons, an allegory of desire redirected toward God

stops.name: Shadiyakh, the Mosibat-nama
stops.campa: In the Mosibat-nama, the Book of Afflictions, Attar sends a solitary wayfarer, the salek-e fekrat, the traveller of Thought, through forty stations of creation in search of relief: he questions Gabriel and the angels, the throne and its pedestal, the tablet and the pen, paradise and hell, sun and moon, the four elements, the mountains and seas, the plants, the animals, the jinn, mankind, the prophets, and at last the faculties of the mind. Each confesses it does not hold what he seeks. Only the universal soul answers him: cast yourself into the ocean of the soul and be utterly effaced, for what you want is nowhere but in you.
suggested_refs: The forty stations of the Mosibat-nama, Attar's darkest and most demanding mathnavi

stops.name: Shadiyakh, Mantiq al-Tayr — the hoopoe calls the birds
stops.campa: In what will become his masterwork, the Mantiq al-Tayr, the Language of the Birds, Attar gathers every bird of the earth in council: they have no king, and the wisest among them, the hoopoe, who once carried letters between Solomon and Sheba, tells them of a king they do have, though none has seen him: the Simurgh, whose feather once fell over China and set every heart there to painting it. Thousands answer the call to seek him; the hoopoe warns that seven valleys of fire and thorn lie between the birds and any sight of their king, and most will not survive the crossing.
stops.quote: The world's birds gathered for their conference / And said: 'Our constitution makes no sense. / All nations in the world require a king; / How is it we alone have no such thing?'
stops.quote_source: Mantiq al-Tayr (The Conference of the Birds), the birds assemble, trans. Afkham Darbandi & Dick Davis
suggested_refs: The hoopoe (hodhod), guide-bird of the Mantiq al-Tayr, carried over from the Qur'anic story of Solomon and Sheba
Two manuscripts give 1177 as the year the poem was finished; its placement late in Attar's working life here is a reconstruction, not a dated fact
sources: The Conference of the Birds, trans. Afkham Darbandi & Dick Davis (Penguin Classics)

stops.name: Shadiyakh, Mantiq al-Tayr — the Simurgh is themselves
stops.campa: Of the thousands who set out, only thirty birds survive the seven valleys, Quest, Love, Knowledge, Detachment, Unity, Bewilderment and Annihilation, to stand at last, stripped of everything, before the court of the Simurgh. There is no king waiting. In the mirror-bright hall they find only their own thirty reflections, and understand, all together, the pun the Persian language has carried the whole poem toward: si morgh, thirty birds, is the Simurgh's own name. The king they crossed the world to find was never separate from the finding; the annihilation of the self and the arrival at God turn out, in the end, to be the same door.
stops.quote: And all who come before My splendour see / Themselves, their own unique reality... / Though you have struggled, wandered, travelled far, / It is yourselves you see and what you are.
stops.quote_source: Mantiq al-Tayr (The Conference of the Birds), closing verses, trans. Afkham Darbandi & Dick Davis
suggested_refs: The Simurgh / si-morgh pun at the poem's climax, later the subject of Jorge Luis Borges's essay 'El Simurgh y el águila'
sources: The Conference of the Birds, trans. Afkham Darbandi & Dick Davis (Penguin Classics)
Jorge Luis Borges, 'El Simurgh y el águila,' Nueve ensayos dantescos

stops.name: Shadiyakh, the Mokhtar-nama and the Pand-nama
stops.campa: In his later years Attar sets down the Mokhtar-nama, more than two thousand quatrains sorted by subject as a concordance to his own thought, and the small, plain-spoken Pand-nama, the Book of Counsel, couplets of household and devotional advice simple enough that generations of Persian schoolchildren after him will learn their letters from its lines. Beside the towering ambition of the birds and their king, these are modest books, but they carry his voice into rooms the mathnavis never reach: the kitchen, the primer, the cheap copied pamphlet sold beside the mosque door for a coin.
suggested_refs: The Pand-nama, used for centuries afterward as a Persian primer for schoolchildren
sources: Pand-nama: Book of Wisdom Selections, various editions

segments.name: The Sea Followed by an Ocean

stops.name: Nishapur, blessed by Attar
stops.campa: An old man now, more than seventy years into a life that began before the Seljuks fell, Attar receives at Nishapur a scholar fleeing west out of Balkh with his household, ahead of a horror gathering in the east that Attar can already half-name. He watches the father walk ahead and the small son trail after, and says, to those standing near, the sentence tradition will not let go: here comes a sea followed by an ocean. He calls the boy to him, puts into his hands his own Asrar-nama, and tells the bystanders this child will soon set fire to the hearts of the world's lovers.
stops.quote: Here comes a sea followed by an ocean.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Farid al-Din Attar on receiving the family of Baha al-Din Valad at Nishapur (Dowlatshah, Tadhkirat al-Shu'ara; Aflaki, Manaqib al-'Arifin)
suggested_refs: rumi.journey.json (the same meeting, from the boy's side, shared pin)
Attar's Asrarnama, given to the child Rumi at this meeting
sources: Franklin Lewis, Rumi: Past and Present, East and West

stops.name: Shadiyakh, news of Otrar
stops.campa: Word reaches Nishapur's caravanserais, a season late as such word always is, of an outrage the year before at the frontier town of Otrar: a trade caravan sent by the Mongol khan Genghis seized on the governor's order, its merchants killed as spies, its goods taken. Traders passing through Attar's own city shake their heads over it as one more of the frontier's usual quarrels, a Sultan's officer overreaching, nothing that need trouble Khorasan's cities deep in the interior. Attar, past seventy now, has outlived enough fires and earthquakes to distrust anyone's certainty that a distant spark will stay distant.
suggested_refs: The Otrar Catastrophe of 1218, casus belli of the Mongol invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire
genghis_khan.journey.json (the caravan's slaughter, shared background event)

stops.name: Shadiyakh, news of Bukhara and Samarkand
stops.campa: Within two years the frontier quarrel has become an empire's ruin: refugees stumbling into Nishapur from the north report Bukhara's great mosque turned into a stable for Mongol horses and its citizens driven before the army as living shields, then Samarkand's citadel, the Sultan's own capital, fallen after the shortest of resistances. Attar, who once walked the roads these very refugees are now fleeing down, listens to their accounts with the attention of a man who has spent a life collecting the last words of the dying. He does not yet know that Khorasan, and his own city, stand next in the line of march.
suggested_refs: The fall of Bukhara and Samarkand, 1220, opening the road to Khorasan
sources: genghis_khan.journey.json (Bukhara and Samarkand, shared background chronology)

stops.name: Shadiyakh, submission to Jebe and Subutai
stops.campa: In May the vanguard of the Mongol advance, under the generals Jebe and Subutai, arrives before Nishapur itself demanding provisions for their march onward toward the fleeing Sultan. The city's council, weighing the fate of Bukhara and Samarkand, opens its gates and supplies what is asked rather than test its walls against the army that has taken both; the generals accept the tribute and ride on in June, leaving Nishapur standing, spared by its own quick submission. Attar, who has seen his city rebuilt once from fire and once from earthquake, watches this newest storm pass by at a distance and, for the moment, without blood.
suggested_refs: The first, peaceful Mongol passage through Nishapur, May 1220, before the city's later rebellion

stops.name: Shadiyakh, Toquchar slain beneath the walls
stops.campa: The peace does not hold. Through the summer, rumors run through Nishapur that the Mongols have been beaten back elsewhere, and the city, encouraged past its own safety, turns on the small occupying garrison left to enforce the khan's writ. In November, Toquchar, son-in-law to Genghis Khan himself, rides up to put down the trouble in person and takes an arrow from the wall for his trouble, dying of the wound before his own camp. Word of a khan's son-in-law killed by Nishapur's own defenders travels back along the Mongol lines faster than any caravan ever carried silk, and it travels with only one possible answer attached to it.
suggested_refs: The death of Toquchar, Genghis Khan's son-in-law, November 1220, the direct cause of Nishapur's destruction

stops.name: Nishapur, the siege of Tolui, three pyramids of skulls
stops.campa: In April, Tolui, Genghis Khan's own son, brings the full weight of a Mongol army against the walls his brother-in-law died beneath, and Toquchar's widow is given the city to do with as she wills. The town that once bought peace with tribute is shown no second mercy: the walls are breached in seventy places, the population put to the sword down to the cats and dogs, the chroniclers say, and the skulls of men, women and children stacked in three separate pyramids. Attar, past seventy-five and still in the city by every report, is among the multitude within the walls when the gates give way.
suggested_refs: The three skull-pyramids of Nishapur, recorded by the Persian chroniclers of the invasion
genghis_khan.journey.json (the same destruction, shared pin)

stops.name: Shadiyakh, the ransom refused
stops.campa: Among the dead and the doomed of the sack, tradition places one particular scene: an old man taken captive by a Mongol soldier, worth something alive to whoever can sell him on. A passerby offers a thousand pieces of silver, and the captor hesitates over the price. It is Attar himself, the story insists, who tells his own captor not to sell so cheap, that a better offer will come. Then another passerby offers a sack of straw, and Attar tells the soldier to take that price instead, for that is exactly what he is worth. Enraged at the silver he has lost, the Mongol kills him where he stands.
stops.quote: Don't sell me as cheaply; you will find someone willing to give more... Sell me to him, for that is all I am worth.
stops.quote_source: Legend of Attar's death in the sack of Nishapur, April 1221, as given in New World Encyclopedia, 'Farid ad-Din Attar' (after Margaret Smith)
suggested_refs: The Mausoleum of Attar of Nishapur, raised at Shadiyakh by order of Ali-Shir Nava'i in the fifteenth century, over the traditional site of his death and burial
sources: New World Encyclopedia, Farid ad-Din Attar
Mausoleum of Attar of Nishapur, Wikipedia
